θάνατον ἐπιποθεῖ, διὰ τὰς ἀνω τέρω λεχθείσας αἰτίας. Πρὸς δὲ διάνοιαν μυστήρια
λαλεῖ· καὶ περὶ τῶν ἤδη προγεγονότων φιλοσοφεῖ, καὶ πληροφορεῖ τὸ μέλλον.
Τοιαῦται γὰρ ἀεὶ τῶν ἁγίων προφητῶν αἱ ῥήσεις. Ἐπὶ δὲ αὐτῶν τῶν λέ ξεων
γενόμενοι, σαφηνίσωμεν τὴν διάνοιαν, αὐτοῦ ποδηγοῦντος πρὸς τὴν ἑρμηνείαν, τοῦ
καὶ τὸν ἅγιον Ἰὼβ πρὸς τοὺς ἀγῶνας ἐνισχύσαντος. Στίχ. αʹ. Μετὰ τοῦτο ἤνοιξεν
Ἰὼβ τὸ στόμα αὐτοῦ. Ὅτι δίκαιος ἀνοίγει τὸ στόμα, οὐχ ἁπλῶς οὑτωσὶ προσήκει
προσέχειν τοῖς λεγομένοις, ἀλλὰ τὰ ἐκ τῶν λόγων ἀναζητεῖν ὠφέλειαν. Μεστὰ γὰρ
ἀεὶ ὠφε λείας τὰ τοιαῦτα ῥήματα τῶν ἁγίων· καὶ ἀνοίγων τὸ στόμα δίκαιος,
κεκρυμμένους δημοσιεύει θησαυ ρούς. ∆ιὸ καὶ τὸ σκεῦος τῆς ἐκλογῆς ὁ Παῦλος ἐπι
στέλλων φησί· Τὸ στόμα μου ἀνέῳγε πρὸς ὑμᾶς, Κορίνθιοι. Καὶ περὶ τοῦ Κυρίου
γέγραπται ὅτι Ἀνοίξας τὸ στόμα αὐτοῦ ἐδίδασκε. Καὶ ἁπλῶς ἐκεῖνος μαρτυρεῖται
στόμα ἀνοίγειν, ὁ σιωπῆς μέτρα πρότερον διδαχθείς. Οὐκοῦν καὶ Ἰὼβ ἀνοίγει τὸ
στόμα 17.69 μετὰ τοῦτο· τουτέστι μετὰ τὸ μέγα τρόπαιον, μετ' ἐκεῖνα τὰ πάθη, οὐκ
ἀβασανίστως φθέγγεται περιαλ γῶν τῷ σώματι, τῆς γλώσσης φθανούσης τὸ τῆς φρο
νήσεως ἔνθεσμον, ἀλλὰ σωφρονῶν καὶ ταῖς φωναῖς ὑποδείκνυται. ∆ηλοῖ δὲ καὶ τὴν
γαλήνην τῆς ψυχῆς καὶ τῶν ῥημάτων τὸ ἐμπρεπὲς ἡ τοῦ ἀνοῖξαι τὸ στόμα αὐτοῦ
μαρτυρία. ΚΕΦ. ΙΘʹ. Στίχ. αʹ. Ἕως τίνος ἔγκοπον ποιήσετε ψυχήν μου; Ὥσπερ σώματα
βαρέα ἐπιτιθέμενα ζώων σώμα σιν, κάμνειν ποιεῖν τὰ βαστάζοντα· οὕτως εἰσί τι νες
λόγοι βαρεῖς, οὓς ἀκούσας τις κάμνει. Ὡς ὑπὸ βάρους πιεζόμενος, τῆς δυνάμεως τῶν
λόγων τῶν οὐ κακῶς, καὶ χαλεπῶς, ἢ ἐπὶ λοιδορίας εἰρημέ νων ὑπὸ τῶν ἄλλων δύο
μετὰ Βαλδὰδ ἐληλυθότων, οἱονεὶ φορτίου αἴσθησις βαρέος, ὁ Ἰώβ φησι καμὼν τῇ
ψυχῇ ἐφ' οἷς εἰρήκασιν· Ἕως τίνος ἔγκοπον ποιήσετε ψυχήν μου; –Καὶ μετ' ὀλίγον·
Ὁρᾷς ὡς προγέγραπται ὁ Σαυχαίων τύραννος. Τυ ραννικοὶ αὐτοῦ εἰσιν οἱ λόγοι, οὓς
ἀκούσας ὁ Ἰὼβ, λέ γει· Ἕω τίνος ἔγκοπον ποιήσετε τὴν ψυχήν μου; Οὐχ οὕτως
καθικνεῖται ψυχῆς ἀνθρώπου ἄλλο τι, ὡς λόγος σκληρός. Πολλάκις ὑπομείνας τὰς
βασάνους σώματι προσφερομένας, λόγους οὐχ ὑπέμεινεν. Ὁ μέντοιγε τέλειος
ἀθλητὴς, εἰ καὶ κάμνων, ἀλλ' ὑπο μένει τοὺς χαλεποὺς λόγους. Ὕβριν γὰρ
ὑπομένειν μεγάλου ἀνδρός ἐστιν. ∆ιόπερ ἐν τοῖς ἀνδραγαθήμα σιν ἑαυτοῦ ὁ
Ἀπόστολος λέγει· Λοιδορούμενοι εὐλο γοῦμεν, διωκόμενοι ἀνεχόμεθα,
δυσφημούμενοι παρακαλοῦμεν. Ὥσπερ καθάρματα τοῦ κόσμου ἐγενήθημεν, πάντων
περίψημα ἕως ἄρτι. Καὶ μετ' ὀλίγον φησὶν εἶτα, διὰ τὸ, Ἕως τίνος ἔγκοπον ποιή σετε
ψυχήν μου; Ὁρᾷς; Ἰώβ ἐστιν, οὗ καὶ τὸ βιβλίον οὐδὲν ἄλλο ἐξαιρέτως περιέχει ἢ τὴν
ἀνδρίαν αὐτοῦ καὶ τὴν ὑπομονήν. Ἀλλ' ὅμως αἰσθάνεται τῶν καμάτων, ὧν κεκμήκει
ἀπὸ τοῦ λόγου τοῦ σκλη ροῦ τῶν ἐληλυθότων αὐτὸν ἐπισκοπῆσαι. Στίχ. γʹ. Γνῶτε
μόνον, ὅτι ὁ Κύριος ἐποίησέ με οὕτως. Ἃ βλέπετε περὶ ἐμὲ, μὴ νομίσητε ἄλλοθεν
ἐληλυ θέναι μοι ἢ ἀπὸ τοῦ Θεοῦ. Φοβήθητε τοίνυν. Ὁ γὰρ ἐμοὶ ταῦτα ἐπάγων
δύναται καὶ ὑμῖν ἐπαγαγεῖν. Στίχ. γʹ. Καταλαλεῖτέ μου· οὐκ αἰσχυνόμενοί με,
ἐπίκεισθέ μοι. Πολλάκις καὶ καταλαλεῖ τις κακῶς ποιῶν. Ὅτε ἂν δὲ οὐκ
ἀπερυθριάσῃ, εἰς πρόσωπον λέγει ἐκείνῳ, οὐχὶ ἐλέγχων, οὐδὲ τἀληθῆ λέγων, ἀλλ'
ὀνει δίζων καὶ ὑβρίζων. Τοῖς γὰρ ὑπὸ Θεοῦ τιμωρου μένοις ἐπεμβαίνειν οὐ χρὴ,
ἀλλὰ θρηνεῖν καὶ φο βεῖσθαι. Στίχ. δʹ. Ναὶ δὴ ἐπ' ἀληθείας ἐγὼ ἐπλανήθην, παρ' ἐμοὶ
δὲ αὐλίζεται πλάνος· λαλῆσαι ῥῆμα, ὃ οὐκ ἔδει. Εἶτά φησιν καθ' ὑπόθεσιν· Ὑμῖν
δίδωμι, ὡς ὑπο 17.72 λαμβάνεται, ὅτι διὰ τὰ ἁμαρτήματα ταῦτα πάσχω· ἆρ' οὖν
ἐχρῆν ὑμᾶς οὕτω μοι ὀνειδίζειν; Παρ' ἐμοὶ δὲ αὐλίζεται πλάνος. Εἰ καὶ καθ' ὑπόθεσιν
τοιαῦτα ἐπεποιήκειν, οἷα οὐκ ἔδει· εἰ καὶ τοιοῦτος ἤμην, ἆρ' οὐκ ἐχρῆν ὑμᾶς
βλέποντας μάστιγας, τοὺς ἰχῶ ρας, τοὺς σκώληκας, τὴν ἀπώλειαν τῶν ὑπαρχόντων,
αἰδεσθῆναι; Ἀλλὰ προσεπιβαίνετέ μοι μὴ ἐλεοῦντές με, μηδὲ συμπαθοῦντές μου τῇ
περιστάσει. Στίχ. εʹ. Ἔα δὲ, ὅτι ἐπ' ἐμοὶ μεγαλύνεσθε, ἐνάλλεσθε δέ μοι ὀνείδει. Οὐ
μετρίως μοι ὀνειδίζετε, ἀλλ' ἐναλλόμενοι ὡσπερεὶ ἐπιβαίνοντες καὶ καταπατοῦντές
με ὀνει δίζετε. Στίχ. ʹ. Ὀχύρωμα δὲ αὐτοῦ ἐπ' ἐμὲ ὕψωσεν. Οἱονεὶ ὑπὸ τεῖχος τῆς
περιστάσεώς εἰμι ὀχύρωμα, ὃ οὐ δύναμαι φεύγειν, ἕως οὗ κρινεῖ ὁ Θεὸς καθελεῖν
αὐτό. Στίχ. ζʹ. Ἰδοὺ γελῶ ὀνείδει, καὶ οὐ λαλήσω. Τοῦτό ἐστι τό· Νίκα ἐν τῷ ἀγαθῷ τὸ
κακόν. Τοῦ αὐτοῦ. Ἰδοὺ ἐπὶ τῷ ὀνείδει ὑμῶν γελᾷν, οὐ λαλεῖν νομίζομαι. ΚΕΦ. Κʹ.
pass_a_gloss: desires death, because of the causes said above. And toward understanding he speaks mysteries; and he philosophizes about the things already having happened, and he assures the future. For such always are the sayings of the holy prophets. And having come upon the words themselves, let us clarify the understanding, he himself guiding toward the interpretation — he who also strengthened holy Job toward the contests. Verse 1: After this Job opened his mouth. That a righteous one opens the mouth — one ought not simply thus attend to the things said, but seek the benefit from the words. For such sayings of the holy ones are always full of benefit; and opening the mouth a righteous one publishes hidden treasures. Therefore also the vessel of election, Paul, writing says: My mouth has opened toward you, Corinthians. And concerning the Lord it is written that Opening his mouth he taught. And simply that one is witnessed to open a mouth who was first taught measures of silence. Therefore Job also opens the mouth 17.69 after this — that is, after the great trophy, after those sufferings — not speaking unexamined while suffering bodily pain, the tongue outrunning the devout measure of prudence, but being shown temperate also in the voices. And the witness of opening his mouth also makes clear the calm of the soul and the seemliness of the words. Chapter 19 verse 1: Until when will you make my soul weary? Just as heavy bodies placed upon bodies of animals make the bearers grow weary, so there are some heavy words which, having heard, someone grows weary. As if pressed by a weight — of the power of the words said not badly, and harshly, or unto insult by the other two who came with Baldad — a perception as of a heavy load, Job says, having grown weary in soul at what they have said: Until when will you make my soul weary? — And a little later: You see how the tyrant of the Saucheans has been written before. Tyrannical are his words, which Job having heard says: Until when will you make my soul weary? Nothing else so reaches a human soul as a hard word. Often having endured the torments brought to the body, one did not endure words. The perfect athlete, however, even if wearying, still endures the harsh words. For to endure insult belongs to a great man. Therefore in his own brave deeds the Apostle says: Being reviled we bless, being persecuted we endure, being defamed we exhort. We have become as the refuse of the world, the offscouring of all until now. And a little later he says then, because of Until when will you make my soul weary? You see? It is Job, whose book especially contains nothing else than his manliness and endurance. But nevertheless he perceives the toils with which he has grown weary from the hard word of those who came to visit him. Verse 3: Know only that the Lord made me thus. What you see about me, do not think has come to me from elsewhere than from God. Fear, then. For the one bringing these things on me can also bring them on you. Verse 3: You speak against me; not being ashamed of me, you press upon me. Often someone also speaks against while doing evil. But when he does not blush, he says to that one’s face — not refuting, nor saying the true things, but reproaching and insulting. For one must not insult those being punished by God, but mourn and fear. Verse 4: Yes indeed, in truth I have wandered; and with me lodges a wanderer — to speak a word which one ought not. Then he says by hypothesis: I grant you, as it is supposed, that because of sins I suffer these things; was it then necessary for you to reproach me thus? And with me lodges a wanderer. Even if by hypothesis I had done such things as one ought not; even if I were such — was it not necessary for you, seeing scourges, the ichors, the worms, the loss of belongings, to feel shame? But you further tread on me, not pitying me, nor sympathizing with my circumstance. Verse 5: But allow that you magnify yourselves against me, and you leap on me with reproach. You do not reproach me moderately, but leaping as if mounting and trampling me you reproach. Verse: And his fortress he raised against me. As if under a wall of the circumstance I am a fortress, which I cannot flee, until God judges to take it down. Verse 7: Look, I laugh at reproach, and I will not speak. This is the: Conquer the evil in the good. Of the same: Look, at your reproach I am thought to laugh, not to speak. Chapter 20.
pass_b_english: desires death for the reasons already given. Toward understanding he speaks mysteries; he philosophizes about what has already happened and assures what is coming — the way holy prophets always speak. Coming to the words themselves, let us clarify the sense, guided by the same one who strengthened holy Job for the contests.

"[[After this Job opened his mouth >> Bible:Job 3:1]]." When a righteous man opens his mouth, do not attend casually; hunt the benefit in the words. Such sayings are always full of help, and a righteous mouth publishes hidden treasures. So the vessel of election writes, "[[My mouth has opened toward you, Corinthians >> Bible:2 Corinthians 6:11]]," and of the Lord it is written that "[[opening his mouth he taught >> Bible:Matthew 5:2]]." The one witnessed to open a mouth is first taught the measures of silence. Job opens his mouth after the great trophy and those sufferings — not letting the tongue outrun devout prudence under bodily pain, but showing temperance in the voices. The witness that he opened his mouth also shows the soul’s calm and the seemliness of the words.

Chapter 19: "[[Until when will you make my soul weary? >> Bible:Job 19:2]]" Heavy loads make beasts weary; heavy words do the same to a hearer. Pressed by the harsh, insulting speech of the other two who came with Baldad, Job feels a heavy load and asks how long they will weary his soul. The Sauchean is labeled tyrant beforehand; his words are tyrannical. Nothing reaches a human soul like a hard word. Many endure bodily torments and still cannot endure speech. The perfect athlete, even weary, endures harsh words; bearing insult belongs to a great man. So the Apostle lists among his brave deeds: "[[Being reviled we bless, being persecuted we endure, being defamed we exhort; we have become as the refuse of the world, the offscouring of all until now >> Bible:1 Corinthians 4:12-13]]." Job’s book especially holds his courage and endurance — and still he feels the toil of hard words from those who came to visit.

"[[Know only that the Lord made me thus >> Bible:Job 19:3]]." What you see about me has not come from elsewhere than God. Fear: the one who brings this on me can bring it on you. "[[You speak against me; unashamed, you press upon me >> Bible:Job 19:3]]." Evil speech happens often; when the speaker does not blush, he says it to the face — not to refute or tell truth, but to reproach and insult. One must not insult those God is punishing, but mourn and fear. "[[Yes, in truth I have wandered; a wanderer lodges with me — to speak a word one ought not >> Bible:Job 19:4]]." By hypothesis he grants their view that he suffers for sins — was it then necessary to reproach him so? Even if he had done what he ought not, seeing scourges, ichor, worms, and lost goods, should they not have felt shame? Instead they tread further, without pity. "[[Allow that you magnify yourselves against me and leap on me with reproach >> Bible:Job 19:5]]" — not moderate rebuke, but leaping as if trampling. "His fortress he raised against me": under the wall of circumstance he is a fortress he cannot flee until God judges to take it down. "[[Look, I laugh at reproach, and I will not speak >> Bible:Job 19:7]]" — that is, "[[conquer the evil in the good >> Bible:Romans 12:21]]." At their reproach he is thought to laugh, not to speak. Chapter 20.
